title: Meaning, Readers, and the Death of the Author
text:
Structuralist criticism holds that meaning arises not from an author's intention but from the system of differences that organizes language itself. Roland Barthes, in his famous essay on the death of the author, argued that a text is a tissue of quotations drawn from innumerable centres of culture. Consequently, the reader, rather than the writer, becomes the site where those fragments are unified. Such a view, though influential, has been criticised for neglecting the historical circumstances in which texts are produced.

Critics of this position often point out that readers do not approach texts in a vacuum. Their interpretations are shaped by class, gender, and the institutions that teach them how to read. Reader-response theorists, by contrast, placed the reader at the centre of meaning-making, though they differed on whether the reader's role was individual or collective. Ultimately, the debate asks whether a text can be said to have a stable meaning at all.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what does structuralist criticism say meaning arises from?
options: The system of differences within language

questions.text: According to the second paragraph, what shapes readers' interpretations?
options: Only their personal taste in literature
Class, gender, and the institutions that teach reading

questions.text: What can be inferred about Barthes's view of the reader?
options: The reader's role is unimportant to meaning.
The reader is the place where a text's fragments are brought together.
The reader should only reproduce the author's intention.
The reader must avoid all cultural references.

questions.text: Why does the passage describe the debate as ultimately unresolved?
options: Because the author never wrote a second text.
Because texts are too short to interpret.
Because critics disagree on whether a text has a stable meaning.
Because readers have stopped reading altogether.

paragraph_translations: La crítica estructuralista sostiene que el significado no surge de la intención del autor, sino del sistema de diferencias que organiza el propio lenguaje. Roland Barthes, en su famoso ensayo sobre la muerte del autor, afirmó que un texto es un tejido de citas extraídas de innumerables centros de cultura. En consecuencia, el lector, y no el escritor, se convierte en el lugar donde esos fragmentos se unifican. Tal visión, aunque influyente, ha sido criticada por descuidar las circunstancias históricas en las que se producen los textos.

Los críticos de esta postura suelen señalar que los lectores no se acercan a los textos en un vacío. Sus interpretaciones están moldeadas por la clase, el género y las instituciones que les enseñan a leer. Los teóricos de la respuesta del lector, en cambio, colocaron al lector en el centro de la construcción del significado, aunque discreparon sobre si el papel del lector era individual o colectivo. En última instancia, el debate plantea si un texto puede tener un significado estable.
